# Kourovka Problem 5.43 (a soluble variety not generated by its finite groups)

The proposition that there are a set $W$ of laws and $d \in \mathbb N$ such that every group satisfying $W$ has derived length at most $d$ (its $d$-th derived subgroup is trivial), and some law $w$ holds in every finite group satisfying $W$ but is not a consequence of $W$ (some group satisfies $W$ but not $w$). Here a law is an element $w$ of the free group $F$ on countably many generators $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$, and a group $G$ satisfies $w$ when every homomorphism $F \to G$ (equivalently, every assignment of elements of $G$ to the generators) sends $w$ to $1$; the variety defined by a set $W$ of laws is the class of groups satisfying every law in $W$.

Source: E. I. Khukhro and V. D. Mazurov (eds.), Unsolved Problems in Group Theory: The Kourovka Notebook, 21st issue, arXiv:1401.0300v49 (2026), Archive of Solved Problems, Problem 5.43 (A. Yu. Olshanskii).
